ABSTRACT
Nanostructured catalysts have been extensively demonstrated for electrochemical CO2 reduction. But, efforts to understand the mechanism of bimetallic catalysts have been limited. Here, we study electronic structures in bimetallic Cu/Ag layered catalysts to eliminate geometrical effects on the electrocatalytic characteristics. We found that the interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag affects the valence electronic states as confirmed by synchrotron radiation photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory calculation. The Ag adatom on Cu surface decreases charge density by forming an additional bond with Cu. As a result, the binding energy of CO intermediate increases on the surface. As the thickness of Ag layer increases, the effect of interfacial interaction of Cu/Ag gradually weakened and the center of d-states downshifted from 4.38 to 5.28 eV. The optimized Cu/Ag layered catalyst exhibited bifunctional catalytic selectivity with high CO faradaic efficiency (FE) = 89.1% at -0.8 VRHE and high methane FE = 65.3% at -1.2 VRHE.
Keywords: Cu-Ag, bifunctional catalyst, carbon dioxide reduction, electronic structure

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) gas into value-added chemicals by electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions (CO2 RR) in aqueous media opens new possibilities for the use of CO2 as a source for energy storage and for mitigating the depletion of fossil fuel.[1-3] However, this vision faces the key challenge of developing highly active and stable electrocatalysts capable of producing a targeting chemical in aqueous electrolytes. Previously, various metals are categorized into three groups based on their product : (i) Au, Ag, Zn, Pd, and Ga, from which carbon monoxide (CO) is the major product;[4-8] (ii) Pb, Hg, In, Sn, Bi, preferentially producing formate (HCOO-);[9-13] (iii) Cu, that is able to produce hydrocarbons.[14-19] Almost metal catalysts have catalytic properties for one product, but only the Cu catalyst can selectively produce CO, methane (CH4), hydrocarbons as well as alcohols depending on the reaction potential. Despite being active for the production of hydrocarbons, Cu catalyst still requires large overpotentials to reduce CO2 and has limited selectivity with faradaic efficiency (FE) less than 50%.[16-19]
Alloying is one of the most promising approaches to improve the selectivity of metal catalysts. It is well known that the binding strength of intermediates could be effectively manipulated to accelerate the CO2 RR because the electronic structure changes by alloying.[20-23] Thus, to improve the catalytic performance of Cu for CO2 RR, research efforts have turned to nanostructured bimetallic catalysts. Over the past several years, various types of high-surface-area Cu-based electrocatalysts such as oxide-derived (OD) electrodes,[24-27] nanoparticles (NPs),[28-31] nanowires,[32-34] and roughened surfaces prepared by electrodeposition and plasma treatments[35, 36] have been investigated. Nanostructured bimetallic Cu catalysts such as Cu-In,[37-39] Cu-Sn,[40-43] Cu-Ag,[44-47] Cu-Au[48, 49] and Cu-Pd[50, 51] weaken the binding strength of CO. Decreasing the binding
4
strength of CO on the surface inhibits further reduction of CO to alcohols or hydrocarbons.[52-54] As a result, high CO faradaic efficiency (FE) up to 90% and high CO partial current density (> -5 mA/cm2) could be obtained. Despite the catalytic properties of CO were improved by using Cu-based bimetallic catalysts, the selectivity towards hydrocarbon is still relatively low.[19] Since Cu is the material that can make various CO2 RR products, design rule is required to achieve high selectivity for CO, CH4 and so on. However, the interpretation of catalytic enhancement of the nanoscale Cu-based bimetallic catalysts is complicated, leading to debates on the active sites and the interplay between electronic and geometric effects. For instance, Cu-Sn bimetallic catalysts with rough surface prepared through the electrodeposition of Sn species on the OD-Cu showed selective CO production (FECO > 90%).[42] On the other hand, Cu-Sn NPs fabricated by solution-based synthesis showed high FE of HCOO- (> 70%).[40] In a recent study, Cu-Ag thin film was prepared by a quench-cooling method using physical vapor deposition.[47] Because these two metals are thermodynamically immiscible, segregated Cu and Ag phases induced compressive strain on the Cu atoms, thereby resulting in increased selectivity of multi-carbon products. But, when two metals are exposed to the electrolyte, the effects of spillover and spontaneous galvanic reaction should also be considered. In short, complicated structure of bimetallic catalysts has been a barrier to understand the catalytic properties. There is a need to derive clear electronic structure-catalytic property relationships without being affected by geometric structure. The relationships would guide the optimization of these complex materials and achieve breakthrough advances.
Here, we demonstrated an experimental approach based on thin film deposition that sheds light on the nature of the electronic structure in Cu-Ag catalysts for CO2 RR. It is known that for the transition metals the coupling between the adsorbate valence states and the metal d-
5
states largely describe the variations in adsorption energy.[20] So, among the various Cubased bimetallic catalysts, we investigated the Cu-Ag system which both two metals have valence d-states. Since the catalytic property of the Cu-Ag catalyst is in principle determined by its electronic structure, the electronic structure was engineered by changing the thickness of Ag layer in Cu/Ag structure. Synchrotron radiation photoelectron spectroscopy (SRPES) and density-functional theory (DFT) calculation evidenced that the interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag changes the electronic structure and the d-states. As a result, by optimizing the Ag thickness, Cu/Ag catalyst has suitable binding energy of CO intermediate and acts as a bifunctional catalyst that is CO selective (FE = 89.1%) at low potential (-0.8 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode, VRHE) and CH4 selective (FE = 65.2%) at high potential (- 1.2 VRHE).

sections.heading: 2.1. Preparation of Cu/Ag layered catalysts
sections.text:
To fabricate the extremely flat Cu foils, the exfoliation method was carried out as follows; Glass substrates with size of 8 x 8 cm2 were cleaned sequentially with acetone, isopropyl alcohol, and deionized (DI) water. After blowing the substrates with air and baking at 110 ºC on a hot plate, Cu thin films (100 nm) were deposited by electron-beam evaporation at a deposition rate of 0.1 nm/s. During the electron-beam evaporation, Cu granules (99.9%, purchased from iTASCO) were melted by irradiation of electron-beam, and then the vaporized Cu was deposited on the glass substrates at a high vacuum of 2 x 10-7 torr and room temperature. To electroplate Cu foils on the glass substrates, the cathode (Cu deposited glass) and anode (99.9% Cu sheet) were electrically connected using a Keithley 2400 digital source meter to ensure the constant current density of 20 mA/cm2 and growth rate of 50 μm/h in the
6
CuSO4-based electrolyte (purchased from Insol Inc.). 100 μm-thick Cu foil could be easily peeled off from the glass substrate. Then, Ag layers with various thicknesses were deposited on the flat Cu foil using an electron-beam evaporator by vaporizing Ag granules (99.99%, purchased from iTASCO). The rate and thickness of Ag layers were in-situ monitored by quart crystal thickness monitor (Fig. S1). Reference Ag foils (99.9%) and Cu foils (99.9%, purchased from Nilaco Co.) were used after cleaning with acetone, isopropyl alcohol, and DI water. 2.2 Characterization
Surface morphology of catalysts was measured using an atomic force microscope operated in tapping mode on a Veeco nanoscope III. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted on 4D beam line at Pohang Accelerator Laboratory (PAL) with a base pressure of 5 10ⅹ -10 Torr and an AXIS Ultra DLD model (KRATOS, U.K.) in an advanced in-situ surface analysis system (AiSAS, KBSI, KOREA) operating at a base pressure of 1.3×10-10 mbar at 300 K with a monochromatic Al Kα line at 1486.69 eV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained from 3D beam line at PAL. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analysis were done using a Cscorrected JEM 2200FS operated at 200 kV. Cross-sectional TEM samples were fabricated by focused ion beam system (SII SMI3050SE). 2.3. Electrochemical measurements
Electrochemical measurements were conducted in an H-type cell separated by a nafion membrane (SelemionTM, Asahi Glass Co.) with a three-electrode system. An Ag/AgCl (purchased from CH Instruments Inc.) filled with 3 M KCl (Sigma-Aldrich) was used for the reference electrode and Pt mesh (99.9%) was used for the counter electrode. The electrolyte used for electrochemical measurements was an aqueous solution of 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sigma-
7
Aldrich, 99.95%) prepared by dissolving the solid salt in DI water. The electrolyte was saturated with CO2 gas before the measurements were performed. The measured potential (VAg/AgCl) (V) could be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE) (V) by using the Nernst function: VRHE= VAg/AgCl + 0.222 + 0.0592 × pH. All the electrochemical measurements were conducted using a potentiostat (Iviumstat, Ivium Technologies) under ambient pressure at room temperature. The active area of prepared sample was 0.283 cm2 and the backside of Cu foil was passivated by sealing tape. 2.4. Product analysis
Gas products were analyzed using a gas chromatography (Inficon, 3000 Micro GC) equipped with two thermal conductivity detectors (TCD) connected to Molsieve column and Plot U column. Before beginning the electrochemical reduction, the apparatus was purged with CO2 gas for 3 min to remove other gases. During the reaction, gas was circulated within the reactor at a flow rate of 50 ml min-1. The reactions for product analysis were conducted for 20 min. After the reaction, gas products were automatically pumped into the gas chromatography for analysis. 2.5. Calculations
First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed with the projector augmented wave (PAW) method and the generalized gradient approximation of Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE) for exchange-correlation potential and implemented in Vienna Ab initio Simulation Pakage (VASP) code.[55, 56] The conventional DFT energy is corrected by Grimme’s method (D3) in order to describe van der Waals interaction properly. Monkhorst-Pack k-point sampling with a grid of 4×4×1 was used for the Brillouin zone integration.[57] An energy cutoff of 500 eV was used for the plane-wave representation of the wavefunctions, and atomic structures were relaxed until all the Hellman-Feynman forces were
8
< 0.01 eV/Å. The slab model for both Cu (111) and Ag (111) was constructed by 80 atoms supercell. More than 15 of vacuum space was employed along the perpendicular direction Å to prevent artificial interaction between the periodic images.

sections.heading: 3.1. Morphology and microstructure of Cu/Ag layered catalysts
sections.text:
In order to study the layered catalyst composed of Cu and Ag thin films, Cu foil with flat surface is primarily required. So, we deposited Cu thin films (100 nm) on glass substrates using electron-beam evaporation method and 100 μm-thick Cu foil was formed by electroplating in CuSO4-based electrolyte. Then, the Cu foil was peeled off from the glass substrate (Fig. 1a). This allows transferring the roughness of glass substrate to the peeled surface of the Cu foil.[58] Since the glass substrate has a smooth surface having average roughness (Ra) of 1.3 nm, the peeled surface of the Cu foil also has a flat surface with Ra = 1.3 nm (Fig. 1b). On the Cu foil substrate, thin Ag layer was deposited via electron-beam evaporation in a high vacuum chamber for fine-tuning of thickness. As confirmed by atomic force microscopic (AFM) images, any noticeable change in Ra was found regardless of Ag thickness (tAg).[59]
In order to determine the thickness required to obtain a continuous Ag layer, Cu LMM Auger spectra were measured by surface-sensitive SRPES (Fig. 1c). Cu foil showed characteristic Cu LMM peaks in the binding energy range of 564 ~ 570 eV. When 1 nm-thick Ag layer was deposited on the Cu foil, the intensity of Cu LMM peaks dramatically decreased because Ag layer screens the photoelectrons emitted from Cu foil. At tAg = 3 nm, Cu LMM peaks completely disappeared and only a strong Ag 3p3/2 peak was observed at 573 eV. This result implies that the 3 nm-thick Ag layer is able to form a continuous Ag thin film covering
9
the entire surface of Cu foil. We analyzed the crystallographic orientation of Cu foil and Ag layer by using synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 1d). Cu foil exhibited polycrystalline microstructure with (111) at 2θ = 43.3º, (200) at 2θ = 50.4º, (220) at 2θ = 74.1º (JCPDS, Cu: 01-0836). When tAg ≤ 5 nm, XRD pattern of Ag layer is not visible because the intensity of Ag layer is below the detection level. At tAg = 10 nm, Ag (111) peak starts to be observed at 2θ = 38.1º, and is very noticeable at tAg = 50 nm (JCPDS, Ag: 04-0783).
Microstructure of Cu/Ag 5 nm catalyst was characterized using cross-sectional transmission electron microscope (TEM). The high-resolution TEM image and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns showed d-spacing of 0.209 nm, 0.181 nm, 0.236 nm, and 0.204 nm, which correspond to the Cu (111), Cu (200), Ag (111) and Ag (200) planes, respectively (Fig. 2a). Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) elemental mapping of Ag and Cu exhibited a distinct boundary between Cu foil and Ag layer, confirming the bilayer structure (Fig. 2b). In the cross-sectional TEM image of Cu/Ag 50 nm (Fig. S2a), it is apparent that Cu foil and Ag layer are polycrystalline composed of many grains having (111) and (100) orientations (Fig. S2b). The 50 nm-thick Ag layer was also uniformly coated on Cu foil without interdiffusion between Ag and Cu (Fig. 2c). These results evidenced that the electron-beam evaporation method enables uniform deposition of Ag layer on Cu foil to the desired thickness.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electronic structure of Cu/Ag layered catalysts
sections.text:
To identify the chemical bonding states between Cu and Ag bilayer, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out. Cu foil showed strong metallic Cu0 peaks at 932.3 and 951.1 eV with small oxide peaks of Cu+ (934.2 and 946.2 eV) and Cu2+ (935.4 and 943.9 eV) (Fig. 3a). The oxide peaks originated from the native oxide formed by exposure to ambient air
10
prior to analysis. As the tAg increases, the intensity of Cu 2p XPS spectra decreased and it disappeared at tAg ≥ 10 nm. In contrast, the intensity of metallic Ag 0 peaks at 368.2 and 374.2 eV gradually increased as tAg increased (Fig. 3b). Compared to Cu/Ag catalysts, Ag 3d peaks of Ag foil shifted to lower binding energy by 0.2 eV and the widths were almost the same. This means that the atomic compositions of Ag layers and Ag foil were nearly identical, but the interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag affect the surface electronic structure. Because the valence band electrons play an important role in catalytic reaction, we measured the valence band spectra for Cu foil, Cu/Ag catalysts, and Ag foil (Fig. 3c). Cu foil showed a strong Cu 3d peak at binding energy of 3.06 eV and all the Cu/Ag catalysts exhibited Ag 4d peak at 4.27 eV. As tAg increases, the density of states between Cu 3d peak and Ag 4d peak decreases gradually. As a result, the d-band center, calculated from the center of gravity from 0 to 9 eV, gradually increases to the binding energy of 4.38, 4.88, 4.93, 4.94, 5.08 and 5.28 eV for Cu foil, Ag 1, 3, 5, 10 and 50 nm, respectively. Because an interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag affects several nanometers away from the interface, the effect of interfacial interaction gradually weakens as tAg increases. Even when the Ag layer (50 nm) was deposited on Cu foil, the valence band spectrum was narrower and the d-band center positioned at higher binding energy than Ag foil. This reveals that the surface electronic structure of the relatively thick Ag layer (50 nm) was still affected by interfacial interaction between Cu foil and Ag layer.
It is important to note that such valence band modification can occur due to electron transfer between Cu and Ag. The driving force for electron transfer is either difference in electronegativity or difference in the number of electrons populated in valence bands.[60] However, Cu and Ag have identical electronegativity and equally filled valence band.[61-64] So, there is no driving force for an electron transfer between Cu and Ag. This was supported
11
by the results that the negligible shift in the binding energies of Cu 2p and Ag 3d spectra, which would be expected if an electron transfer occurs between Cu and Ag. Instead, we explain that the reason for valence band modification is decreased charge density by forming an additional bond between Ag with Cu. The effect of charge redistribution and downshift of d-band center on binding energy of CO intermediates would be discussed in the following experimental and DFT calculation sections.

sections.heading: 3.3. Electrochemical CO2 reduction
sections.text:
Faradaic efficiency (FE) (Fig. 4a-d), partial current density (Fig. S3a,b) and production rate (Fig. S3c,d) of Cu, Ag and Cu/Ag catalysts were characterized at different applied potentials from -0.4 to -1.2 VRHE in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. Cu foil mainly produced hydrogen with FEH2 of 85.7% at low potential (-0.4 VRHE) and FEH2 gradually decreased to 29.4% at high potential (-1.1 VRHE) (Fig. 4a and Table S1). The maximum FECO was as small as 21.3% at the moderate potential of -0.8 VRHE and a relatively large amount of methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4) were produced with FECH4 = 44.0% and FEC2H4 = 13.6% at the high potential of -1.1 VRHE, respectively. Ag foil began to produce CO at -0.6 VRHE, and the maximum FECO was 72.3% at -0.9 VRHE. As the potential increased to -1.2 VRHE, FECO gradually decreased to 14.4%, and FECH4 increased to 17.8% (Fig. 4b). When the thin Ag layer (3 nm) was deposited on the Cu foil, FEH2 decreased below 20% (Fig. 4c). On the other hand, the maximum FECO dramatically increased to 89.1% at -0.8 VRHE, and FECH4 also remarkably increased to 65.3% at -1.2 VRHE. In the case of thick Ag layer (50 nm), FECO was 81.0% at -0.8 VRHE and 90.9% at -0.9 VRHE (Fig. 4d).
In order to compare the selectivity of CO2 reduction products of CO and CH4, the difference of faradaic efficiency (FECO-FECH4) was plotted as a function of the potential (Fig.
12
4e). Cu foil showed selective CO production (FECO-FECH4 = 17.0%) at -0.8 VRHE and CH4 production (FECO-FECH4 = -40.5%) at -1.2 VRHE. Compared to Cu foil, Ag foil exhibited higher FECO selectivity (FECO-FECH4 = 72.3%) at -0.9 VRHE and lower CH4 selectivity (FECOFECH4 = -3.4%) at -1.2 VRHE. When the thin Ag layer (3 nm) was deposited on Cu foil, the Cu/Ag 3 nm catalyst is highly CO selective (FECO-FECH4 = 89.1%) at -0.8 VRHE and highly CH4 selective (FECO-FECH4 = -53.1%) at -1.2 VRHE. It is noteworthy that Cu/Ag 3 nm is an excellent bifunctional catalyst that enables the selective production of both CO and CH4 by changing the applied potential. The thick Ag layer (50 nm) on Cu foil showed CO selective characteristic with a negligible amount of CH4 production. Interestingly, Cu/Ag 50 nm catalyst revealed higher CO selectivity than Ag foil. This means that the narrowing and the shift of valence band to higher binding energy, originated from interface interaction between Cu foil and Ag layer, altered the catalytic performance and improved the CO selectivity.
We measured the FE (Fig. 4f) and production rate (Fig. S4) of CO and CH4 at -0.8 and -1.2 VRHE with tAg. At -0.8 VRHE, FECO gradually increased to 89.1% with increasing tAg and nearly saturated until tAg = 50 nm (Table S2). At -1.2 VRHE, FECO was drastically suppressed below 10% while FECH4 gradually increased to the maximum value of 66.0% at tAg = 3 nm, and then decreased as tAg further increased. Based on the selective production of both FECO and FECH4 at tAg = 3 nm, we believe that the Cu/Ag 3 nm has an optimized electronic structure for the bifunctional catalysts. Electrochemical surface area of the Cu/Ag catalysts exhibited similar values regardless of tAg (Fig. S5), indicating that the change in the catalytic activity originated from intrinsic material properties rather than surface morphology.
In order to demonstrate whether the Cu/Ag layered catalysts function as bifunctional catalysts on commercial Cu (Cml Cu) foils, we compared the catalytic performance of flat Cu and Cml Cu. The flat Cu, fabricated by peeling off the electroplated Cu foil from the glass
13
substrate, has a smooth surface (Fig. 5a). Accordingly, the flat Cu/Ag 3 nm also showed a smooth surface. On the other hand, Cml Cu and Cml Cu/Ag 3 nm samples exhibited rough surface with rolling marks. In addition to the surface roughness, flat Cu and Cml Cu have different crystallographic orientations; Flat Cu has (111) preferred orientation with small (200) and (220) XRD peaks (Fig. 5b). But, Cml Cu has a strong (220) XRD peak with relatively negligible (111) and (220) peaks. Because of the difference in microstructure, flat Cu showed better CO2 reduction selectivity on both CO (FE = 21.4% at -0.8 VRHE) and CH4 (FE = 43.5% at -1.2 VRHE) than Cml Cu (FECO = 4.3% at -0.8 VRHE and FECH4 = 28.8% at -1.2 VRHE) (Fig. 5c and Table S3). Despite flat Cu and Cml Cu have different catalytic activity of CO2 reduction, Cu/Ag 3 nm layered catalysts showed similar CO and CH4 FEs regardless of Cu substrate; Flat Cu/Ag 3 nm and Cml Cu/Ag 3 nm showed FECO = 89.1%, FECO = 93.1% at - 0.8 VRHE and FECH4 = 65.2%, FECH4 = 59.2% at -1.2 VRHE, respectively. It is noteworthy that the Cu/Ag layered catalysts exhibit bifunctional properties without being affected by the crystal orientation and surface roughness of the Cu substrate. From this result, we believe that the ligand effect due to the electron redistribution between interfacial Cu and Ag is superior to the strain effect that is sensitive to the crystal orientation.
To further investigate the Cu/Ag layered catalyst, CuxAg100-x thin films (3 nm) were deposited on Cu foil with varying weight percentages of Cu and Ag (Fig. S6a). Comparing to Cu/Ag 3 nm catalysts, the Ag-rich layer (Cu5Ag95) exhibited a little decrease in CO selectivity (FECO = 72.0%) at -0.8 VRHE and a large decrease in CH4 selectivity (FECH4 = 32.1%) at -1.2 VRHE (Fig. S6b and Table S4). A small amount of Cu (5 wt%) exposed on the catalytic surface dramatically decreased CH4 selectivity. In comparison, the Cu-rich layer (Cu95Ag5) with a small amount of Ag (5 wt%) showed much higher CO selectivity (FECO = 58.9%) than pure Cu layer (FECO = 8.1%). A small amount of Ag (5 wt%) effectively promote the CO
14
generation. Although it was found that a small amount of exposed Cu reduces the selectivity of CH4 and a small amount of exposed Ag improves the CO selectivity, Cu/Ag layered catalyst showed the best bifunctional characteristics among the prepared samples. We believe that Cu/Ag layered structure has different catalytic nature than Cu-Ag alloys.[46, 47] Also, the bifunctional catalyst properties are a special feature of Cu/Ag layered catalysts, which were not observed in Cu/Au layered catalysts of the same structure (Fig. S7 and Table S5). It is expected that the bifunctional catalytic properties can only be realized by the interaction between Cu and Ag.
We conducted chronoamperometric measurements of Cu/Ag 3 nm layered catalysts for 12 h at constant potentials of -0.8 and -1.2 VRHE in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Fig. S8). CO2 gas was kept bubbled in the electrolyte to prevent the changing of the pH value during the reaction. The sample exhibited nearly constant current densities of ~1.0 mA/cm2 at -0.8 VRHE, and ~5.9 mA/cm2 at -1.2 VRHE for 12 h of reaction, indicating stable electrical properties.

sections.heading: 3.4. DFT calculation and interpretation
sections.text:
First-principles DFT calculations were employed to understand the enhanced selectivity of both CO and CH4 molecules on Cu/Ag 3 nm catalyst surface. For the study, we first looked at the binding energy of CO and CH4 molecule on Cu and Ag surfaces. Since Cu foil and the Ag layer in this study preferentially grows on [111] direction as confirmed by XRD patterns, the binding energy on (111) surface was mainly considered. Fig. 6a shows the binding energy of CO and CH4 on (111) surface plane of Cu and Ag. We note here that the most energetically favorable site for CO is on-top site for Ag (111) surface and face-centered-cubic site for Cu (111) surface (Fig. S9). Our DFT results predict that the CO binding energy is much higher on Cu surface (1.02 eV) than on Ag surface (0.40 eV). Thus, Cu forms much strong binding with
15
CO than Ag. On the other hand, the CH4 binding energy is weak on both surfaces; the calculated CH4 binding energy is 0.25 eV on Cu and 0.18 eV on Ag. Hence, CH4 can be easily desorbed from both surfaces once it is produced. We further looked at the binding energy of Ag adatom (Agad) on Cu surface with CO and CH4 in order to understand how much the binding energy changes when Ag atom places on Cu surface. The calculation results show that the binding energy of Agad is 0.71 eV for CO and 0.18 eV for CH4. Thus, the adsorption between Agad and CO molecule is quite strengthened while that with CH4 remains weak.
In order to understand the reason for a change of CO binding energy, charge states of surface atoms (Ag, Cu and Agad) were investigated. For the study, bader charge analysis,[65] which assigns the charge density by dividing atoms along zero flux surfaces, is performed. Our results show that the charge on Cu (9.852 e) is lower than that of Ag (10.143 e). It seems that lower charged Cu forms strong binding with CO molecule than Ag. On the other hand, Agad on Cu surface decreases its charge density by forming an additional bond with Cu (Fig. 6b). As a result, the charge on Agad decreased from 10.143e to 10.091e, and accordingly, the binding energy increased from 0.40 eV to 0.71 eV. We further investigate the change in CO binding energy as a function of electron deficiency on Ag (111) surface to verify our calculation result. For the study, the electron deficiency on surface Ag was achieved by subtracting electrons from the entire slab system. DFT study clearly shows that the CO binding energy is proportional to the electron deficiency on Ag atom (Fig. S10). The CO binding energy gradually increases from 0.40 eV and reaches to 0.77 eV with 0.023e decrease of the electron density on Ag atom. Although the values are not exactly matching with the case of Agad on Cu, we can clearly see that the decrease in the electron density on Ag atom increases the CO binding energy. Thus, we have successfully verified that the electron deficiency of Agad by forming additional bonds with Cu plays a key role in the tailoring the
16
electronic structure and the adsorption strength of CO intermediate on the catalytic surface.
It is well known that the d-band center model is regarded as an efficient activity descriptor for noble-metal catalysts. As confirmed by valence band spectra, the d-band center in Cu/Ag bilayer catalysts is downshifted from the Fermi level as tAg increases. The lower energy of the d-band center would possibly lead to weaker bonding between the adsorbates and metal surfaces because the antibonding states of absorbate are more filled with electrons (Fig. 7a). The CO binding energies calculated by DFT calculation can explain why catalytic selectivity varies significantly on different surfaces. For Cu surface, the CO binding energy is more than 1 eV. On the other hand, the overpotential that yields the formation of CH4 is less than 1 eV. As a result, the CO will preferentially convert into CH4 before it desorbs from the Cu surface. Unlike Cu surface, the CO binding energy is only 0.4 eV on Ag surface. This means that CO molecule can desorb from the Ag surface before it is converted into CH4. Thus, Cu/Ag 50 nm surface exhibits high CO selectivity since Ag film shows the bulk-like property. For the Cu/Ag 3 nm catalyst, however, the CO binding energy is 0.71 eV which is slightly lower than the energy required for the CH4 conversion. As a result, the CO can either be desorbed from the surface when overpotential reaches the CO binding energy or convert into CH4 when the overpotential provides sufficient energy for subsequent hydrogenation of CO to generate CH4 (Fig. 7b). As a result, the Cu/Ag 3 nm catalyst can show the bifunctional catalytic behavior.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we derived correlations of catalytic performance with the electronic structure in Cu/Ag catalysts. In order to eliminate the structural effect of a nanostructure, Cu/Ag layered catalysts were conducted. It was found that the interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag affects the electronic structure of the surface. As the thickness of Ag layer increases, the
17
center of d-states gradually downshifted from the Fermi level, thereby resulting in weak CO binding energy on the surface. The optimized Cu/Ag layered catalyst exhibited bifunctional catalytic characteristic which preferentially produces CO (FECO = 89.1%) at -0.8 VRHE and has high selectivity of CH4 (FECH4 = 65.3%) at -1.2 VRHE. This study sheds light on the mechanism of interfacial interaction of bimetallic catalysts that results in the enhanced CO2 RR performance and provides a guideline to design the electronic structure of multicomponent electrocatalysts.

Highlights
Bifunctional Cu/Ag layered catalyst were fabricated by physical vapor deposition of Ag layer on the Cu foil. Electronic structure was engineered by changing the thickness of Ag layer. Interfacial interaction between Cu and Ag changes the electronic structure and the dstates at valence band. Cu/Ag layered catalyst is CO selective (faradaic efficiency, FE = 89.1%) at moderate potential (-0.8 VRHE) and CH4 selective (FE = 65.2%) at high potential (-1.2 VRHE).
